articleTitle: Meta’s Muse AI Agent Mixing Conversations and Exposing Private Data, Internal Reports Show

claims.claim: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

claims.claim: In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

claims.evidence: Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told TechCrunch that “employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public,” and Roberts described Reuters’ examples as “isolated incidents.” Ars Technica quoted a Meta staffer writing “Hmmm,” after Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden, and Ars Technica also quoted the staffer’s out-of-context output about a coffee table pickup that “doesn’t seem to be yours.”

claims.claim: A security firm, Claroc, discovered that the chat‑sharing feature in Muse exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records.
claims.bestSource: Meta Employees Raise Muse AI Privacy Concerns, Exposing Security Flaws, Chat Leaks
claims.evidence: Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed.Separately, security firm Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature in Muse exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records. Claroc discovered that Muse’s chat-sharing feature exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records, and Claroc found that users who shared a conversation did not realize the resulting links were discoverable by anyone with the right DNS query.
claims.bestPassage: Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed.Separately, security firm Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature in Muse exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records. Claroc discovered that Muse’s chat-sharing feature exposed shared conversations through publicly searchable DNS records, and Claroc found that users who shared a conversation did not realize the resulting links were discoverable by anyone with the right DNS query.

claims.claim: Researchers needed a single DNS query to surface thousands of previously shared chat links, all of which were accessible to anyone who found them, without any login requirement.
claims.bestSource: Meta Employees Raise Muse AI Privacy Concerns, Exposing Security Flaws, Chat Leaks
claims.evidence: Security researchers needed a single DNS query to surface thousands of previously shared chat links, all of which were accessible to anyone who found them, without any login requirement.The exposed conversations were created by users who had explicitly chosen to share them with specific recipients but did not expect that those links would be discoverable by third parties.
